newsitem.title: CHINA: China starts unloading backlog of sleeping shares.
newsitem.headline: China starts unloading backlog of sleeping shares.

text.p: China's decision to list a further batch of the companies involved in the 1980s issue frenzy has hit domestic A shares and still leaves a question mark over millions of other shares, analysts said on Thursday.

More than 4,000 companies issued shares to their workers or institutions through private placements in the latter part of the 1980s as part of Beijing's attempt to reform its loss-making state industrial sector.
Fearing that the wave of issues was getting out of control, Beijing imposed a ban in the early 1990s, leaving millions of investors holding shares in companies with no prospect of being listed.
"Most of the companies are small, commercial trading firms which are not suitable for listing," said a stock analyst with Shenyin & Wanguo Securities.
"But the problem involves millions of investors, prompting the central government to take measures to solve it."
"The problem has been on the agenda since early last year," said an economist with China Financial Trust and Investment Co. "The solution has now basically been worked out."

In 1995, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), the top securities watchdog, and the State Commission for Economic Restructuring evaluated the firms concerned and decided that 90 could be listed.
Since late last year, 26 of the 90 have been listed, including Cai Hong Display Devices in Shanghai and Chongqing Traditional Chinese Medicine in Shenzhen.

A CSRC notice issued on Tuesday last week said the securities authorities planned to list 32 more of the companies before the end of next year, prompting the Shanghai and Shenzhen domestic A share markets to fall sharply on the day.
Shenzhen's A share index tumbled a further 5.32 percent on Wednesday this week, while Shanghai A shares lost 2.04 percent in part on rumours A share listings would be accelerated, brokers said.
The criteria used for determing which companies should be listed have never been openly revealed and a CSRC spokeswoman on Thursday said that it was not allowed to make them public.
"The listing of these shares has caused a quick expansion of the A share markets, depressing prices," said one trader with China Guotai Securities.
"But these firms have been carefully selected, with a few investors holding most of their shares. They are suitable for listing and will help activate the markets," he added.

On Tuesday, government departments issued a circular saying the rest of the more than 4,000 companies which had issued the unlisted shares should buy them back from investors. It did not specify what the re-purchase price should be.

The circular said that if a firm could not afford to buy them back, shares owned by retail investors must be collected and be entrusted to a securities house. It did not say if the securities company would have to pay for them.
Those firms which found it difficult to continue operating should apply for bankruptcy or be wound up.
"The settlement of the so-called 'problems left over from history' will help China's stock market and the national economy as a whole in the long run," one banking analyst said.
"But these problems have also raised questions on how China should reform its state-run industrial sector and the central government seems to have no ready answer yet."
